meaning: Fearlessness; the state of being free from dread, born of recognizing the non-dual Self.
Non-duality; the philosophical school holding that individual consciousness (Ātman) and cosmic ground (Brahman) are identical.
One of the oldest Mukhya Upaniṣads, belonging to the Ṛgveda, containing the Mahāvākya 'Prajñānaṃ Brahma'.
The Imperishable, unalterable; also refers to the indestructible sacred syllable OM.
The physical sheath made of food and nourishment; the gross biological body.
The causal sheath of bliss and joyful peace experienced in deep sleep and contemplation.
The innermost Self; pure witnessing consciousness that remains invariant across all states of mind.
etymology: Root an- (to breathe) or at- (to go/pervade)

meaning: Primordial ignorance; metaphysical unawareness of one's true nature as non-dual consciousness.
Scholarly commentary on root philosophical scriptures (such as Śaṅkara's Upaniṣad-bhāṣyas).
The Infinite, the Immense; that unconditioned plenum in which alone true bliss resides.
The infinite, unchanging, all-pervasive ground of all existence and consciousness.
The 'Great Forest' Upaniṣad; the longest and one of the oldest principal Upaniṣads (Śukla Yajurveda).
Discriminative intellect; higher executive faculty capable of discernment, wisdom, and decision-making.
Major ancient Upaniṣad belonging to the Sāmaveda, renowned for 'Tat Tvam Asi' and the Nārada-Sanatkumāra dialogue.
Mind-stuff; the repository of memory, subconscious impressions (saṃskāras), and cognitive flux.
Restraint of the external sensory organs; sensory discipline preventing compulsive reactivity.
Compassion, tender empathy toward suffering beings; one of the three thunder-commands.
Generosity, charitable giving; detachment from possessive hoarding.
Fortitude, calm resilience, unshakable inner composure born of spiritual wisdom.
The steadfast, wise person who remains unshaken amidst pleasures and distress.
Dualism; philosophical school founded by Madhvācārya holding eternal distinction between God, soul, and world.
Spiritual teacher who dispels darkness; guide on the contemplative journey.
Sense organ; five cognitive senses (jñānendriya) and five active organs (karmendriya).
The 'Lord' Upaniṣad; brief 18-verse opening of the Śukla Yajurveda Saṃhitā emphasizing engaged renunciation.
The waking state of consciousness; outward sensory perception of the gross physical realm.
The empirical individual living soul, temporarily conditioned by body and mind.
Transformative direct wisdom or spiritual realization, distinguished from factual accumulation.
Action, deed; also the psychodynamic law of moral cause and effect.
Principal Upaniṣad telling the story of Nachiketa and Yama, containing the chariot allegory.
etymology: Name of a Vedic sage / recension

meaning: Principal Upaniṣad opening with 'By whom impelled?'; investigates the conscious power behind the senses.
Sheath or layer enveloping the pure Self in the Taittirīya psychological model.
13th-century philosopher-theologian who founded the Dvaita (dualist) school of Vedānta.
Great spiritual proclamation; four premier statements in the Upaniṣads declaring non-duality.
Late classical Upaniṣad known for profound psychological analysis of mind and yogic breath regulation.
Rigorous rational reflection and intellectual examination to resolve doubts regarding sacred teachings.
The lower emotional and sensory mind; processes incoming sense data and oscillates in desires.
The mental/emotional sheath consisting of reactive thought, desire, and feelings.
Condensed 12-verse Upaniṣad analyzing OM and the four states of consciousness (waking, dream, deep sleep, Turīya).
The creative power of projection; the empirical world of appearance that conceals non-dual truth.
Liberation from ignorance, limitation, and the cycle of suffering; the supreme human goal.
The principal 10 to 13 ancient Upaniṣads commented upon by Śaṅkarācārya.
Principal Upaniṣad (Atharvaveda) containing the 'Two Birds' allegory and 'Satyam eva jayate'.
Deep meditative assimilation; resting continuously in non-dual realization until it becomes spontaneous baseline.
The primordial sacred syllable representing the totality of consciousness across all dimensions of time.
The five sheaths of human personality (Annamaya, Prāṇamaya, Manomaya, Vijñānamaya, Ānandamaya).
Pure Awareness, luminous wisdom; consciousness as the foundation of all reality (Aitareya Up.).
Vital life-force; biological and psychic breath that animates physical and emotional functions.
The vital energy sheath consisting of the five physiological breaths and autonomic life currents.
The three canonical foundations of Vedānta: Upaniṣads (Śruti), Bhagavad Gītā (Smṛti), and Brahma Sūtras (Nyāya).
The pleasant, immediate gratification; worldly indulgence that seems attractive but leads to bondage.
11th-century theologian-philosopher who founded the Viśiṣṭādvaita (qualified non-dualism) school.
Seer, sage; ancient contemplative poet who directly perceived eternal cosmic truths.
The pure witness; transcendent observing consciousness that notices all thoughts and emotions without involvement.
Single-pointed mental focus; integration of cognitive faculties upon spiritual truth.
The endless wandering cycle of mundane existence, birth, death, and existential friction.
Truth, reality; unvarnished truthfulness in thought, word, and action; ontological reality.
Tranquility, mastery of mental agitations; down-regulation of internal emotional churn.
Adi Śaṅkarācārya (c. 8th century CE), premier philosopher-reformer of Advaita Vedānta.
Student, disciple; earnest seeker under the guidance of a spiritual teacher.
Existential trust, deep conviction in truth, sincere intellectual and spiritual faith.
Attentive listening; receptive, open absorption of sacred philosophical wisdom from teachers and texts.
The good, highest welfare; spiritual excellence and enduring wisdom (contrasted with Preyas).
That which is directly heard; primordial revealed literature consisting of the Vedas and Upaniṣads.
Person of steady, unshakeable wisdom who remains balanced in joy and grief (Bhagavad Gītā 2.54–72).
The deep, dreamless sleep state; temporary dissolution of mental objects into undifferentiated peace.
The dreaming state of consciousness; inner subjective creation of subtle mental worlds.
Spiritual heat, disciplined inquiry, focused contemplative austerity.
Patient endurance; capacity to bear pairs of opposites (heat/cold, praise/censure) without mental collapse or retaliation.
The Fourth; unconditioned witnessing consciousness underlying and illuminating waking, dream, and deep sleep.
Sitting near a teacher with devotion; secret spiritual wisdom that loosens bondage and destroys ignorance.
etymology: upa (near) + ni (down) + sad (to sit / to loosen)

meaning: Quiet withdrawal from worldly busyness; psychological detachment from sensory distractions.
The intellectual sheath consisting of discriminative intellect (buddhi) and reflective wisdom.
Qualified non-dualism; school of Vedānta expounded by Rāmānuja wherein souls and world form the body of God.
Discrimination; the capacity to distinguish the permanent from the impermanent, Self from non-Self.
Union; steady control of the mind and senses (Kaṭha 2.3.11); integration of consciousness.
